questions.q: What is the null hypothesis of a Granger test for 'X Granger-causes Y'?
options: The coefficients of the lags of X are all zero
X and Y are the same series
Y is a random walk
X is white noise
why: Correct: if all the X coefficients are zero, X adds no predictive power.
Identical series are not the idea of the test.
A random walk is not the null here.
The test does not assume anything about X being noise.

questions.q: RSS_r = 90, RSS_u = 80, p = 2, and N-(2p+1) = 80. What is F?
In statsmodels grangercausalitytests(data, maxlag), which column is tested as the possible cause?
options: The second column
The first column
Both columns at once
The index
why: Correct: it tests whether the second column Granger-causes the first.
The first column is the target.
You have to run it in both directions.
The index is not used as a variable.

questions.q: Which problem can make X 'Granger-cause' Y without a real effect?
options: A hidden variable Z that drives X first and Y later
Using too many data points
A negative coefficient
Using the F-test instead of a t-test
why: Correct: X acts as an early signal of Z, so it helps to predict Y, but it does not cause Y.
More data helps the test.
The sign of the coefficient does not matter for the test.
The F-test is the right test for several coefficients at once.

questions.q: Why do we run Granger tests on differenced data when the series trend?
options: Trends cause spurious results in the regressions
Differencing makes the F value larger
The test cannot run on positive numbers
Differencing removes the need for lags
why: Correct: non-stationary data breaks the assumptions of the test and creates fake links.
We do not difference to get a larger F. We difference to get a valid F.
The test works on any real numbers.
Lags are still needed.

questions.q: A test finds that web traffic Granger-causes sales (p = 0.01). Your manager asks 'so if we buy more traffic, sales will go up?' What is the best answer?
options: Traffic helps to predict sales, but to know the effect of buying traffic we need an experiment
Yes, it is proven
No, Granger tests are always wrong
Only if p is below 0.001
why: Correct: prediction is not intervention. A controlled test is needed for the effect of a change.
Granger causality does not prove cause and effect.
The test is useful for prediction. It is not always wrong.
A smaller p-value does not turn prediction into cause.

questions.q: Which situation is hard for a Granger test?
options: X affects Y inside the same time step (instant effect)
X affects Y one step later
Y depends on its own past
X is stationary
why: Correct: the test uses past values of X, so a same-step effect is not visible.
This is the case the test is made for.
The restricted model already handles this.
Stationary X is what we want.
